transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-06 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Sam Patel (Redwood AE), Riley Chen (Redwood SE), Annie Vu (Redwood), Maya Rodriguez (Stratus), Omar Khan (Stratus), Priya Menon (Stratus), Luca Ferrer (Stratus), Jin Wu (Stratus)

Auto Summary (auto gen may be incomplete): discuss private vpc connectivity, instance access options, egress patterns, resolver breakage and runtime kv cache locality, agree to run lab

00:00 Sam Patel: hey everyone, thanks for doing this deep dive um we've got Riley and Annie from our side to run through the networking and runtime pieces. can you all intro quick?
00:14 Maya Rodriguez: yeah thanks sam, I'm Maya, head of platform at Stratus we manage infra and the inference rollout. Omar is our infra lead, Priya is security, Luca SRE, jin is product.
00:28 Riley Chen: awesome, quick agenda: access patterns (ssm vs bastion), nat egress and hairpinning, resolver / dns pathing, then runtime notes for kv cache and batching. we'll leave time for lab planning.
00:45 Omar Khan: quick context — our cluster is multi-az in aws, private subnets only, we use nat-gw per-az for egress, and we have strict egress whitelists. we prefer no public bastion.
01:05 Priya Menon: sec requirement: no inbound internet access to nodes, audit logs, kms for keys, soc2 controls. we need to ensure redwood private control plane hooks don't open new ingress.
01:25 Riley Chen: yep that maps. first topic — instance access: we generally recommend SSM Session Manager for ops and debug because it avoids public bastions and you can tie to KMS and IAM. SSM also supports port forwarding for ephemeral tunnels.
01:43 Maya Rodriguez: so SSM will require ssm agent and appropriate role policies, right? we were worried about mTLS to the control plane — will that create egress to redwood endpoints?
01:58 Sam Patel: good question. for Private deployments we give a private control plane option — you can route control-plane egress via privatelink or specific resolvers. we'll share the documentation. link: https://redwood.infra/docs/private-vpc-checklist (note: placeholder)
02:18 Riley Chen: practically you'll need to allow outbound to SSM endpoints (or use VPC endpoints for SSM). If you want zero internet egress we advise VPC endpoints for ssm, ec2messages, and ssm messages. We also support SSM proxy patterns in air-gapped setups.
02:37 Omar Khan: got it. what about file transfer and port forwarding? we need to pull logs to a central s3; do you recommend VPC endpoint for S3 or relay through an egress proxy?
02:51 Annie Vu: s3 VPC endpoints are typical. Some customers put an egress proxy for logging to enforce TLS interception and ACLs. Redwood's logging can be shipped via a push model if you prefer not to pull.
03:08 Riley Chen: ok moving to NAT hairpin and source/dest checks — there's been some weirdness where inference runtime does internal callbacks to other cluster nodes for kv cache invalidation, and if the route table forces egress through nat-gw that can hairpin and add 20-50ms per round trip.
03:27 Luca Ferrer: that's our pain point — cross-az kv miss causes a hop out to nat and back, spikes latency. we've seen p95 token latency jump 70ms in worst case.
03:44 Riley Chen: yep. options: 1) ensure internal traffic uses VPC internal routes (i.e. route table not forcing egress for intra-vpc), 2) use an egress design with nat-gw per subnet and proper routing, 3) put kv cache co-located with inference pods or use local redis per-az.
04:05 Omar Khan: option 3 sounds expensive. what about using source/destination check disable on an ENI and a proxy?
04:12 Riley Chen: can work — using a NAT instance or appliance you can do hairpin without extra egress charges, but it's operational overhead. NAT gateway per AZ with correct route tables usually simplest. but ensure you don't have a default route to nat that captures internal service CIDRs.
04:35 Maya Rodriguez: our current problem is resolver failover — when primary resolver goes down our pods ask external resolver and tokens spike. can you walk through the split-horizon resolver pattern?
04:50 Riley Chen: sure. we recommend deploying a VPC-local resolver (dnsmasq or route53 resolver endpoints) that forwards private names to internal control plane and egress names to the firewall. Use route53 inbound/outbound endpoints for hybrid. For high availability, use multi-az resolvers with failover TTLs — also ensure the nodes have multiple resolv.conf entries (two local resolvers) so failover is fast.
05:20 Priya Menon: is there a recommended TTL and retry policy? we need to ensure no long stalls for the runtime when resolver flips.
05:30 Riley Chen: short TTL like 30s for dynamic records, but for the control plane you can keep longer. For runtime DNS resolution inside the model server, we advise using a local caching resolver (nscd or dnsmasq) to avoid per-request external resolution. Redwood runtime has a built-in dns cache option that respects negative TTLs.
05:50 Sam Patel: also note, KV cache locality — language model runtimes are sensitive to KV latency; a handful of ms adds up across many tokens. design to keep kv lookups inside the AZ when possible.
06:07 Omar Khan: can you quantify? if kv lookup is 5ms vs 30ms what's the token impact?
06:15 Riley Chen: rough math — each new token requires attention queries and potential kv hits; a 25ms delta per token scales linearly. for streamed responses you might see added latency and throughput drop. In our benchmarks, cross-AZ kv lookups cost about 15-40% throughput loss depending on model size and batching.
06:38 Jin Wu: batching profiles: we want high throughput but low p95 latency, how do you tune concurrency and batch sizes?
06:45 Riley Chen: first pick target p95 latency SLO. Then set concurrency per instance so that average batch forms at, say, 30-50ms wait window. If you target low latency (<200ms p95) keep concurrency small and batch timeout low. If throughput matters more, increase batch window and concurrency. Also enable prefix caching to reduce kv hits for repeated prefixes.
07:10 Luca Ferrer: prefix caching — does it need sticky sessions? we're using k8s service with round robin and we're worried about kv cache warmness across pods.
07:20 Riley Chen: good point. we support two patterns: sticky sessions to affinity by user session or KV warmup pre-population. For scale, we recommend dividing traffic by shard keys so cache hotness stays local. We can also enable cross-pod prefetch of common prefixes during rollout.
07:40 Maya Rodriguez: quantization — will q4x and q8_0 change eviction behavior for kv? any gotchas?
07:47 Riley Chen: quantization mainly affects compute and memory; kv cache is orthogonal but note smaller quantized models may change tokenization patterns and thus cache hit rates. Also some quant libraries alter kernel sizes which change per-token compute; ensure your GPU driver and runtime kernels support the quant profile. We'll provide a compatibility matrix.
08:10 Sam Patel: Riley will share the quantization runbook and compatibility matrix after this call.
08:18 Omar Khan: talk to me about canary rollouts and model pinning in private — we want to test new quantized model variants without impacting prod.
08:27 Annie Vu: Redwood supports model pinning per route; you can specify rollout percentages and set fallback to a stable variant. For private deployments we provide offline image packages so you can stage the model locally. Canary traffic can be routed by header or by sampling in the ingress.
08:45 Priya Menon: and audit logs for these rollouts? our auditors will want to see who executed model swaps and when.
08:52 Sam Patel: we log rollout events and provide audit trails; for private we integrate with your cloud logging and can emit to a dedicated s3 or kinesis.
09:05 Maya Rodriguez: okay the egress path — sometimes our VPC endpoints resolve to public IPs via NAT and that breaks privatelink routing. any tips?
09:18 Riley Chen: ensure split-horizon DNS and route53 private zones so privatelink endpoints resolve to private IPs. If your resolver forwards externally you'll get public IPs and then NAT egress will hit the firewall. Also validate that the control plane privatelink is mapped to the same VPC region and the route table has a target to the VPC endpoint.
09:42 Omar Khan: we ran into an MTU issue with nlb and privatelink where large tokens stream hit fragmentation and caused retries. what's the typical MTU setting you advise?
09:52 Riley Chen: generally 1500 is fine but with ipsec tunnels or VPNs you may need to reduce to 1400-1420. For streaming responses consider doing PMTU discovery and set keepalive chunk sizes to avoid fragmentation. We'll add an MTU checklist to the test plan.
10:12 Maya Rodriguez: another real-world issue — hairpin DNS when pods call back to the same service hostname and the resolver returns the public interface. This caused external egress and subsequent firewall blocks. How to detect that quickly?
10:25 Riley Chen: traceroute from pod to hostname, check dig +short inside pod and compare to pod IPs. We recommend an automated healthcheck that verifies internal names resolve to private IPs and that connection path stays inside VPC. We'll include probe scripts in the lab artifacts.
10:45 Jin Wu: cost question — multi-az nat-gw per az is expensive; any lower cost options for high availability and avoiding hairpin?
10:55 Riley Chen: cheaper option is a NAT instance with autoscaling and EIP failover, but it's management heavy. Some customers put an egress appliance in each AZ with cheaper instances. Balance cost vs ops complexity. For scale the managed NAT gateway is simplest and less error-prone.
11:12 Luca Ferrer: for the kv cache locality, if we do per-az redis, how do you handle cache coherence for cross-az sessions?
11:22 Riley Chen: prefer eventual consistency for KV caches — design for eventual misses and warmups. If you need strongly consistent global state use a different store and accept latency. For inference KV we typically use per-az caches and accept occasional misses.
11:40 Priya Menon: security checklist — we need SSO integration and RBAC for control plane operations, plus KMS for model keys. Do you support ccm/bring-your-own-kms?
11:49 Sam Patel: yes BYOK via customer-managed KMS is supported in Private; for SSO we integrate with SAML/OIDC and can map roles to RBAC. We'll send the security pack.
12:05 Maya Rodriguez: okay let's plan the lab — we want to reproduce hairpin latency, resolver failover, and a quantized model rollout in a dev env. Can you outline test cases?
12:18 Riley Chen: test cases we'll provide: - KV cross-az miss path timing - hairpin tracing when route table misconfig - dns resolver flip test (primary down) - streaming MTU fragmentation test - quantized q4x vs float baseline throughput comparison - canary routing and rollback test
12:38 Sam Patel: we'll share a lab plan doc and a small terraform module to stand up the env. We'll also include the traceroute and dns probe scripts.
12:52 Omar Khan: timeframe? we can start next week for the internal runs and then set a 2h lab with your SREs the following week.
13:00 Sam Patel: sounds good. any blockers from security?
13:05 Priya Menon: need the security pack and network flows matrix for audit before we let external engineers in.
13:12 Sam Patel: we'll send that. action items recap in the chat.
13:25 Riley Chen: last note on runtime — consider setting cache eviction policy to LRU with slightly larger capacity to minimize cold misses during rollout and enable prefix caching for repeated prompts.
13:40 Maya Rodriguez: thanks everyone. let's sync on results by next Tue.
